content: The studies reviewed here primarily focused on the relationship between breastfeeding duration and various health outcomes. However, many were excluded from analysis due to not studying the effects of continued breastfeeding. For example: 1. Weyermann (2006) analyzed breastfeeding durations of less than 3 months, 3 to less than 6 months, 6 to less than 9 months, and 9 months or more but did not study continued breastfeeding. 2. Whaley (2017) used logistic regression to assess the impact of breastfeeding duration on obesity but excluded continued breastfeeding from the analysis. 3. Whitmore (1993) compared breastfed children with those never breastfed and treated lactation duration as a continuous variable but did not examine continued breastfeeding. 4. Wienfield (2020) focused on diet quality as an outcome, which was not relevant to the analysis of continued breastfeeding. 5. Wiklund (2012) defined prolonged breastfeeding as more than 10 months but did not study continued breastfeeding. 6. Woo (2008) and Wright (2000, 2001) categorized breastfeeding durations but excluded continued breastfeeding from their analyses. 7. Wu (1996) was a case-control study with cases selected from various institutions, making it unsuitable for studying continued breastfeeding. 8. Yang (2018) and Yazdani (2011) analyzed breastfeeding duration as a continuous variable but did not include continued breastfeeding. 9. Yazici (2011) divided participants into groups based on breastfeeding duration but excluded continued breastfeeding. 10. Yelverton (2020) studied child eating behavior, which was not relevant to continued breastfeeding. 11. Yokoi (2020) defined prolonged breastfeeding as more than 18 months but did not include continued breastfeeding in the analysis. 12. Yonezu (2006) lacked a comparison group and only studied children with continued breastfeeding. 13. Yuan (1988) and Yun (2016) analyzed cumulative lactation durations but excluded continued breastfeeding. 14. Zhang (2003, 2004a, 2017) and Zhao (2020) categorized breastfeeding durations but did not study continued breastfeeding. 15. Zhou (2007, 2012) and Ziegler (2003) analyzed breastfeeding durations but excluded continued breastfeeding. 16. Zielhuis (1989) and Zive (1992) categorized breastfeeding durations but did not study continued breastfeeding. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Studies were rated as high, moderate, low, or very low quality based on the likelihood that further research would change confidence in the effect estimates. For example: Lima (2019) and Stuebe (2010, 2009) faced similar issues, including missing data and confounding. Nguyen (2019) and Ki (2017) were downgraded for indirectness, as their study populations were from single countries, limiting generalizability. Overall, the evidence highlights the need for more robust studies specifically examining the effects of continued breastfeeding on health outcomes. Many existing studies either excluded this variable or had methodological limitations that reduced the reliability of their findings.
